title: Distributed variational quantum computing with deterministic entanglement tuning
authors: Ilhwan Kim, Yong-Su Kim, Kwang Jo Lee, Hyukjoon Kwon, Yosep Kim, Hyang-Tag Lim
abstract: Distributed quantum computing offers a scalable route to quantum information processing by entangling spatially separated processors. Although gate teleportation enables universal computation across distributed nodes, it requires repeated consumption of high-fidelity Bell pairs, ancillary qubits, and real-time feedforward, which imposes significant overhead and reduces fidelity. However, many variational quantum algorithms do not demand full universality; rather, they rely on sufficient expressibility to explore solution spaces effectively. Building on this, we propose a distributed variational quantum computing protocol based on deterministic entanglement tuning. In contrast to probabilistic filtering, our approach deterministically modulates pre-shared entanglement using only local operations and classical communication. We validate the protocol through a proof-of-principle experiment by estimating ground-state energies of the He-H$^+$ molecule and the Schwinger model, showing that diverse entanglement levels can be engineered to match problem-specific requirements. Our results suggest a practical alternative for near-term distributed quantum applications.
summary: This work presents a novel, deterministic protocol for tuning entanglement in distributed quantum computing using photonic qubits. By replacing probabilistic filtering with a LOCC-based measurement operation, the authors enable precise control over the quantum resource. This method is experimentally validated by accurately estimating the ground-state energies of complex molecular and lattice models.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of creating a scalable and practical protocol for distributed variational quantum computing (DVQC) that avoids the high overhead of full gate teleportation.
main_result: A deterministic entanglement tuning protocol was successfully demonstrated, allowing the engineering of specific entanglement levels required by the problem, and this was validated by estimating ground-state energies for benchmark Hamiltonians.
method: The protocol uses deterministic entanglement tuning, which modulates pre-shared entanglement using only local operations and classical communication (LOCC), avoiding probabilistic postselection.
model_or_system: The experiment is performed on a photonic DVQC setup using polarization-entangled photon pairs distributed to two spatially separated nodes (Alice and Bob). The tuning mechanism involves a displaced Sagnac interferometer.
key_observables: Concurrence (to quantify entanglement), Success Probability, and the estimated ground-state energies ($\langle H angle$) for the He-H+ molecule and the Schwinger model.
important_parameters: The tuning parameter $	heta$ controls the degree of entanglement, and the results are benchmarked against theoretical predictions for molecular and lattice Hamiltonians.
main_assumptions: The protocol assumes starting with a sufficiently entangled resource (Bell pairs) and notes that the current implementation requires offline correction for feed-forward.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the DVQC protocol schematic, the experimental linear-optical setup, and show the measured concurrence and energy estimates for the benchmark problems.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the limitations of current DVQC methods, proposes the deterministic entanglement tuning protocol, details its implementation using photonic hardware, and validates the approach by applying it to estimate ground-state energies of molecular and lattice Hamiltonians.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete, hardware-validated method for resource management in distributed quantum computation, which is crucial for scaling up quantum simulations beyond single nodes.
